doc.title: Skitch Henderson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Milford, Connecticut, October 31, 1998

title: Why the swing era ended
summary: Amplifiers, bebop, rock and the changing sense of time.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: What’s your take on why that era ended so quickly?

I don’t know, because none of us knew it was ending, at least I didn’t. I wasn’t intelligent enough to know it was happening. I think the amplifier of course was one of the death © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

nails, I feel. I mean it’s funny, I lived and worked in New York at NBC and I watched this, because when I shed the band I went back to NBC with Sinatra and was doing the Lucky Strike Show and it was the beginning of — what would you say, rock and — contemporary, I don’t know what term you use. And I sat there at 30 Rockefeller Plaza and didn’t have the — I’d go listen but I couldn’t understand it. And I watched Bebop go through. I watched all of that go through. It was so hard for me to — I must say it was hard for me to assimilate it. And maybe that was the problem. Maybe all the men, because there weren’t many women, all the men that lived through that era, maybe they were just so stunned by the change. And didn’t time have a lot to do with it, that’s again the time factory. I can’t complain because I watched my kids, I tried to watch or listen through their eyes. Everything was time. Rock was time. Even The Beatles was time.
Yeah. Something happened. And that Renaissance to almost the style of Mozart you know, it was a very strange Renaissance.
